incumbent

in-KUM-bunt — stress the KUM; an incumbent is already comfortably settled into the office. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Incumbent is currently holding a particular office or position.

The incumbent mayor faced two challengers in this year's election.

Example

A senator has held her seat for twelve years. This November, the incumbent is running again, and campaign signs remind voters that she already knows how the job works, unlike her opponents.

She is the one currently holding the office and seeking to keep it. Unlike 'popular,' which describes how well-liked someone is, incumbent simply names the fact that a person currently occupies the position.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

sitting: Sitting states the plain fact that someone currently occupies an office — the sitting judge, the sitting president. Incumbent says the same thing but belongs to the language of elections: the incumbent is the current holder measured against challengers, often defending the seat. Every incumbent is sitting; incumbent adds the contest.

reigning: Reigning describes someone currently holding a title, especially a champion who keeps it through continued victory — the reigning chess champion. Incumbent belongs to offices and elections rather than titles won by performance: an incumbent mayor holds a position voters granted, not a crown defended match by match.

presiding: Presiding means currently in charge of a particular meeting, courtroom, or ceremony while it is happening — the presiding judge runs today's trial. Incumbent describes holding the office itself across its whole term. A judge presides over one session; the incumbent judge holds the seat until the next election.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

former: having previously held a position, no longer in it

challenger: someone competing to take a position from its current holder

Where it sits · how firmly the office is held — established → incumbent → entrenched

established vs. incumbent: Established is weaker than incumbent — an established figure is simply well-known and experienced, while an incumbent specifically and currently holds the office in question.

entrenched vs. incumbent: Entrenched is stronger than incumbent: an incumbent official currently holds the office, but an entrenched one has held it so long that removing them seems almost impossible.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-

prefix — in-: upon (Latin)

root — -cumb-

root — -cumb-: to lie down, to recline (Latin)

suffix — -ent

suffix — -ent: in a state of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin incumbere meant 'to lie down upon, to press upon.' An incumbent official is one currently 'resting upon,' or occupying, the office.

Use the root in a new word: succumb

Use the root in a new word: succumb: Despite her best efforts, the tired runner finally began to succumb to exhaustion near the finish line.
